# Julia essentials for modelers {#sec-julia-essentials}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 1, Session 1. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

This prerequisite equips you with the specific slice of Julia that the rest of
the course depends on: functions with in-place mutation, broadcasting and
comprehensions, named tuples for model parameters, multiple dispatch, and
reproducible random numbers. Rather than surveying the language, we introduce each feature
through the object we return to in every chapter — the susceptible–infectious–
recovered (SIR) model of @kermack1927.

Scientific computing has long been split across two languages: a convenient one
for writing the analysis and a fast one for the parts that turn out to be too
slow. Julia is designed to be both. It is dynamically typed and interactive like
R, but compiles to native code, so the model kernels you write in this course
are the same code that runs inside the solvers — nothing is rewritten in C to
make it fast enough [@bezanson2017]. @roesch2023 makes the same case for
computational biology at more length. That matters here because epidemic
models are run thousands of times over, in stochastic ensembles, sensitivity
sweeps, and inference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Coming from R?

Most of what you know transfers directly. Assignment uses `=` rather than `<-`,
and indexing starts at 1 as it does in R.

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `v[1]` | `v[1]` | indexing starts at 1, as in R |
| `m[2, ]` | `m[2, :]` | row 2, every column; `:` is all of a dimension |
| `sapply(v, f)` | `f.(v)` | the dot applies `f` elementwise |
| `sapply(1:5, f)` | `[f(k) for k in 1:5]` | a comprehension builds a vector |
| `x[x < 0.5]` | `x[x .< 0.5]` | comparisons need the dot too |
| `for (i in 1:10)` | `for i in 1:10 ... end` | no brackets, closed with `end` |
| `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `(a = 1, b = 2)` | a named tuple; read fields with `p.a` |
| `rbinom(1, n, prob)` | `rand(Binomial(n, prob))` | build the distribution, then draw |
| `TRUE` / `FALSE` | `true` / `false` | lowercase |

An R named list also translates to a `Dict`, `Dict("a" => 1)`, read with
`d["a"]`; this course uses named tuples for model parameters because their field
names are known to the compiler. The official
[noteworthy differences from R](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/noteworthy-differences/#Noteworthy-differences-from-R)
is the complete list.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- read and write Julia functions that mutate a preallocated array in place, the
  form this course uses for every model kernel;
- use broadcasting (`.`) and comprehensions to vectorise scalar operations
  without writing loops;
- group model parameters in a `NamedTuple` and access them by field rather than
  by position;
- collect results with a loop and `push!` or into a preallocated array, and
  build a variant parameter set with `merge`;
- recognise that Julia resolves a function by the *types* of its arguments, and
  explain why that is what lets `solve` accept a compatible problem/algorithm
  pair without glue code;
- draw the same random numbers on every machine with `StableRNGs`, and say what
  that does and does not guarantee about what you compute from them;
- say what a macro does to your code before that code runs, and use
  `@macroexpand` to see the result;
- explain why a derivative of your own model is available without rewriting
  it in another library's operations;
- name the route by which Julia code calls R, Python or C, and what a
  crossing costs;
- render a figure from code with `CairoMakie`.

## Model assumptions and classification

The running example is the deterministic SIR model. It assumes a closed,
well-mixed population of fixed size $N$, split into susceptible $S$, infectious
$I$, and recovered $R$ compartments. Individuals mix homogeneously, each
contacting others at rate $c$; a contact between a susceptible and an infectious
individual transmits with probability $\beta$; infectious individuals recover at
constant rate $\gamma$ and are then permanently immune.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Deterministic |
| Time | Continuous |
| State | Continuous |
| Representation | Population (compartmental) |

We do not solve the model here — that is @sec-foundations. In this unit the
model is a vehicle for the Julia constructs you will reuse throughout.

## Equations

The force of infection is $\lambda(t) = \beta c I(t)/N$, and the compartmental
rates of change are

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda S, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda S - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I.
$$ {#eq-p01-sir}

Because the three right-hand sides sum to zero, the total population is a
conserved quantity:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(S + I + R\right) = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(t) + I(t) + R(t) = N.
$$ {#eq-p01-conservation}

When we later discretise time we will need to turn a continuous rate $r$ into
the probability that at least one event occurs in a window of length $\delta t$,
assuming events follow a Poisson process:

$$
p(r, \delta t) = 1 - e^{-r\,\delta t}.
$$ {#eq-p01-rate}

## Julia implementation

We use the course baseline scenario $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$,
$c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, $\gamma=0.25$.

### The REPL and its modes

Julia's read–eval–print loop is the interactive prompt you get by running
`julia`, and it plays the role the console plays in R. What is unusual is that
it has four modes rather than one. Each is entered by typing a single character
at an empty `julia>` prompt, and left again with `Backspace`:

| Key | Mode | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| — | Julia | evaluating expressions; the default |
| `?` | help | `?expm1` prints a function's docstring, signatures, and examples |
| `]` | package | `]st` shows the active environment, `]instantiate` installs it |
| `;` | shell | run `ls`, `cd`, or `git status` without leaving Julia |

```
julia> 2 + 2
4

help?> expm1
  expm1(x)

  Accurately compute exp(x) - 1.

(EpiModelingCourse) pkg> st StableRNGs
Status `~/modeling-epidemics-julia/Project.toml`
  [860ef19b] StableRNGs v1.0.3

shell> ls prerequisites
01-julia-essentials.qmd
```

The prompt in package mode names the *active environment*, and that name is the
first thing to check when a package appears to be missing. The course's packages
are declared in the repository's `Project.toml`, and Julia does **not** pick that
up merely because you started it in the repository folder: a plain `julia` starts
in your default environment, which knows nothing about them. Start with
`julia --project=.` from the top of the repository, or press `]` and run
`activate .`, then `instantiate` once to install what the project declares.
Only then does `using CairoMakie` resolve.

The first `using CairoMakie` in a fresh session takes a minute or more while
Julia compiles the plotting stack, and once per session after that it is fast.
[Setting up](../setup.qmd) covers this and the rest of the installation.

Help mode is worth building a habit around. Most Base and package functions carry
a docstring, so `?` answers most "what arguments does this take"
questions faster than a web search, and it works offline on the exact version
you have installed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Typing Greek letters

The course writes parameters as `β`, `γ`, and `λ` so the code matches the
equations. These are ordinary variable names, entered at any Julia prompt or in
an editor with a backslash-name and Tab: `\beta`⇥ gives `β`, `\gamma`⇥ gives
`γ`, `\lambda`⇥ gives `λ`, and `\delta`⇥ gives `δ`. Subscripts work the same
way, and the next chapter uses them for $R_0$ and $s_0$: `R\_0`⇥ gives `R₀` and
`s\_0`⇥ gives `s₀`. ASCII names such as `beta` and `R0` work identically — the
choice is cosmetic.
:::

### Functions and in-place mutation

A SciML right-hand side can be written two ways. The *out-of-place* form
`f(u, p, t)` builds and returns a new derivative vector each time it is called.
The *in-place* form `f!(du, u, p, t)` instead *writes* the derivatives into a
preallocated vector `du` and returns nothing, which avoids allocating a fresh
array on each of the thousands of evaluations a solver makes. Both are supported;
this course uses the in-place form throughout, so that is the one to get fluent
in. Here `u = [S, I, R]` maps directly onto the states in @eq-p01-sir, and `p`
carries $(\beta, c, \gamma, N)$.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-kernel
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N     # force of infection, λ = βcI/N
    du[1] = -λ * S              # dS/dt
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I     # dI/dt
    du[3] = p.γ * I             # dR/dt
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]        # S, I, R
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
du = zeros(3)
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)
du
```

The trailing `!` is a Julia convention marking a function that mutates its
arguments.

Note the two containers are read in different ways, and this is the convention
the whole course follows. The state `u` is a plain vector whose order is fixed
by @eq-p01-sir, so we destructure it positionally: `S, I, R = u`. The parameters
`p` are a `NamedTuple`, read by field: `p.β`, never `p[1]`. Parameter lists grow
and get reordered as models gain features, and a positional read fails silently
when that happens — the code still runs and every number is wrong. A field name
either resolves or errors.

### Broadcasting and comprehensions

The dot syntax applies a scalar function elementwise, fusing a chain of dotted
operations into a single loop. What that saves is the *intermediate* arrays a
chain would otherwise build one step at a time; the result array is still
allocated. To write into an array you already have, use `.=`, as the
preallocation example below does. We use broadcasting constantly to evaluate a
model over a grid. Below we compute @eq-p01-rate for a range of window widths and two
rates.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-broadcast
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)   # numerically stable 1 - exp(-r δt)

δts = 0.0:0.05:2.0
p_fast = rate_to_proportion.(1.0, δts)   # broadcast over δts
p_slow = rate_to_proportion.(0.25, δts)
(first(p_fast), last(p_fast), first(p_slow), last(p_slow))
```

`expm1(x)` computes $e^x - 1$ accurately for small `x`, avoiding the
cancellation error of `1 - exp(...)`.

A *comprehension* is the other way to build a vector from an expression. Where
broadcasting applies one function elementwise, a comprehension can evaluate an
arbitrary expression per element, so it is what we reach for when the body is
more than a single call:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-comprehension
prevalences = [10.0, 100.0, 500.0]
[p.β * p.c * I / p.N for I in prevalences]     # λ at three prevalences
```

Read it right to left: *for each* `I` *in* `prevalences`, evaluate the
expression, and collect the results into a vector. We use comprehensions
throughout the course to sweep a parameter or to pull one compartment out of a
solved model.

### Building and updating containers

Broadcasting and comprehensions cover the case where one expression is applied
to every element. When the body is longer, or when a result has to be assembled
along the way, we write the loop out and collect as we go. An empty typed array
grows with `push!`:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-loop
contact_rates = [4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0]
reproduction_numbers = Float64[]

for c_val in contact_rates
    push!(reproduction_numbers, p.β * c_val / p.γ)   # R₀ = βc/γ
end

reproduction_numbers
```

`Float64[]` is an empty vector whose element type is fixed when it is created.
Plain `[]` gives a `Vector{Any}`, which the compiler cannot specialise on, so the
element type is always worth naming. The loop variable is `c_val` rather than
`c`, because `p.c` is already the contact rate and shadowing it makes the body
harder to read.

When the number of results is known in advance, allocate the array once and fill
it by index. Later chapters store whole trajectories this way, one row per
compartment and one column per scenario or time step:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-preallocate
prevalences = [10.0, 100.0, 500.0]
derivatives = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, length(prevalences))

for (k, I) in enumerate(prevalences)
    sir_ode!(du, [p.N - I, I, 0.0], p, 0.0)
    derivatives[:, k] .= du
end

derivatives
```

`undef` leaves the memory uninitialised, so every entry has to be written before
it is read. `enumerate` pairs each element with its position, which is where the
index `k` comes from. The `.=` copies into the existing column instead of
replacing it, the same in-place idea as `du[1] = ...` above. Reading back,
`derivatives[:, k]` is column `k`, and `derivatives[2, :]` is
$\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$ at all three prevalences: this row slicing is how the
course pulls one compartment out of a stored trajectory.

A `NamedTuple` cannot be modified in place, so a scenario that changes one
parameter is built with `merge`, which returns a new tuple with the named fields
replaced and the rest carried over:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-merge
p_low = merge(p, (c = 4.0,))
(baseline_c = p.c, low_c = p_low.c, β_carried_over = p_low.β == p.β)
```

The trailing comma in `(c = 4.0,)` is what makes it a one-field named tuple;
without it the brackets are ordinary grouping and `merge` has nothing to merge.
This is how the course varies one parameter at a time, including from inside a
solver callback (@sec-ordinary-differential-equations).

`map` applies a function to each element and collects the results, like a
comprehension with a function in place of the expression. A `do` block writes
the function body after the collection, which keeps a multi-line body readable:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-map-do
sweep = map(contact_rates) do c_val
    p_c = merge(p, (c = c_val,))
    (c = c_val, R₀ = p_c.β * p_c.c / p_c.γ)
end
```

Each iteration returns a small `NamedTuple`, so `sweep` is a vector of rows,
which is the shape a parameter sweep is usually reported in.

The validation cells in every unit ask a question of a whole collection at once.
`all`, `any` and `count` take the test first and the collection second:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-predicates
(any(>(1), reproduction_numbers),
 count(>(1), reproduction_numbers),
 all(v -> isapprox(sum(v), 0.0; atol = 1e-12), eachcol(derivatives)))
```

`>(1)` builds the function "is greater than 1", and `v -> isapprox(...)` is an
anonymous function, written inline because it is needed once. `eachcol` walks
the columns of the matrix, so the third check reads as "the derivatives conserve
population at every prevalence".

### Multiple dispatch

Multiple dispatch lets one function name resolve to different *methods*
depending on the types of its arguments. A method is one concrete
implementation; the function is the name they share. Here `force_of_infection`
accepts either the number infectious or a whole state vector, from which it
reads $I$ itself:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-dispatch
force_of_infection(I::Number, p)         = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
force_of_infection(u::AbstractVector, p) = force_of_infection(u[2], p)

(force_of_infection(10.0, p), force_of_infection(u0, p))
```

`Number` and `AbstractVector` are *abstract* types — categories rather than
concrete containers — so the second method accepts any vector-like argument, not
just the `Vector{Float64}` we happen to pass. Note what dispatch replaces: there
is no `if` inspecting what was passed in, and no extra argument saying which form
the caller used.

You will not often write dispatch in this course, but you will rely on it in
every chapter. When the next chapters call `solve(prob, Tsit5())`, no glue code
connects that problem to that algorithm: `solve` resolves to a method chosen by
the types of *both* arguments. This is why swapping `Tsit5()` for another
compatible ODE solver needs no change to the kernel you wrote, and why the same
`ODEProblem` usually goes straight to a sensitivity or inference package. One
exception is worth knowing before you meet it: some automatic-differentiation
backends cannot differentiate through code that writes into arrays, and want the
out-of-place kernel instead. The section on differentiating code you wrote
yourself, below, says what that machinery is. What dispatch cannot do is invent
a combination nobody has written, and that is what "compatible" means above:
`solve` works for
the pair in front of it because some package defines a method for those two
types.
Independently written SciML packages compose because each adds methods rather
than editing anyone else's.

### From text to machine code

The sections that follow all depend on what Julia does between the moment you
press Enter and the moment a number comes back. It happens in three stages.

**Reading.** Julia first turns the text you typed into a structured object
called an *expression*. The expression records what the code means rather than
how it was spelled: `β * c * I / N` becomes a small tree with the operations at
the branches and the names at the leaves. Spacing and comments are gone by this
point. Putting a colon in front of code gives you the expression instead of the
result, and `dump` prints its structure:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-ast
dump(:(x + 1))
```

The head says what kind of thing this is, here a function call, and the
arguments are the function `+`, the name `x`, and the number `1`. This
representation has a standard name, the *abstract syntax tree*: a tree because
operations nest inside operations, syntax because it mirrors the structure of
what you wrote, abstract because the formatting has been dropped.

An expression is an ordinary value, so you can take it apart and put it back
together before running it:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-ast-rewrite
e = :(2 + 5)
e.args[1] = :*
eval(e)
```

**Rewriting.** That is the mechanism behind the next section. Anything
beginning with `@` is a *macro*, a rule that receives the expression and
returns a different expression to be used in its place.

**Compiling.** Julia then translates the expression into native machine
instructions for your processor, and does this separately for each combination
of argument types the function is called with. This is where multiple dispatch
feeds in. Knowing that `S` holds a `Float64` and not some unspecified value
lets the compiler emit a single machine multiply rather than a lookup while the
program runs. It is also why calling a function with a type it has never seen
does something useful, which the section on differentiation relies on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The same idea in R

R exposes its own syntax trees, and the same three steps work there:

```r
my_expr <- quote(2 + 5)
as.list(my_expr)          # [[1]] `+`  [[2]] 2  [[3]] 5
my_expr[[1]] <- quote(`*`)
eval(my_expr)             # 10
```

`lobstr::ast(y <- x * 10)` draws the tree, and `substitute` is what lets
`plot(x, y)` label the axes with the names you passed rather than their values.
A formula such as `y ~ x + z` is the same device: `~` quotes what is written on
either side instead of computing it, which is how a modelling function receives
your terms rather than their values. Inspecting and rewriting code before it
runs is not a Julia distinction.

The difference is the third stage. R's just-in-time compiler turns your
function into *bytecode*, an instruction set that R's own virtual machine reads
and carries out one instruction at a time, calling into R's precompiled C
routines as it goes. Julia compiles to instructions your processor runs
directly [@bezanson2017]. The same rewriting mechanism that gives R users a
convenient formula interface therefore gives Julia users a modelling notation
that runs at full speed.
:::

### Macros and modelling notation

Names beginning with `@` appear in nearly every later chapter:
`@reaction_network` in @sec-reaction-networks, `@model` in
@sec-bayesian-inference, `@agent` in @sec-agent-based-models. These are macros,
and a macro is not a function you call. It is a rewrite applied to your code
before the code runs.

A function receives *values*: by the time `f(x + 1)` reaches `f`, the addition
has happened and `f` sees a number. A macro receives the *expression* `x + 1`
itself, unevaluated, and may do anything with it, including discarding it or
turning it into fifty lines of something else. Writing one is not needed
anywhere in this course. Reading one takes a few lines:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-macro
macro log_and_run(ex)
    println("about to run: ", ex)
    return esc(ex)
end

@log_and_run 10 * 20
```

The `println` happens while the code is being prepared, not while it runs. What
the macro returns is what executes, and `@macroexpand` shows you what that was:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-macroexpand
@macroexpand @log_and_run 10 * 20
```

The message appears again because expanding the macro is what runs the
`println`. The multiplication does not: `@macroexpand` stops at the expression
the macro handed back, without evaluating it. Point it at any of the package
macros below and you get the same thing, a few dozen lines longer.

That is what lets a package offer notation that is not ordinary Julia.
Catalyst's `@reaction_network` accepts reaction arrows [@loman2023]:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-reaction-network
using Catalyst

sir_network = @reaction_network begin
    β * c / N, S + I --> 2I
    γ,         I     --> R
end
nothing
```

`-->` is a real Julia operator that no function gives a meaning to, so
`S + I --> 2I` is an expression Julia can represent but cannot evaluate. The
macro supplies the meaning, reading it as a reaction and generating the
corresponding equations. Nothing about that is private to the package: the
equations can be printed, and they are the ones we wrote by hand above.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-reaction-equations
equations(ode_model(sir_network))
```

A package defining notation this way is offering a *domain-specific language*:
a small vocabulary specialised to one subject, here chemical and
epidemiological reactions. `@macroexpand` prints the code a macro generated,
which is how you check what a line of that vocabulary became.

Other languages reach some of the same ground by *operator overloading*, and
if you have used `cvxpy` or `sympy` in Python you have seen it. There, `<=` and
`+` are given new meanings for a special kind of object, and calling them
builds a description of the model instead of computing with numbers. It works
well and it has two limits. It only reaches operators
the language already has, so it cannot give you `-->`, or `~` meaning "is
distributed as" inside a model block. And the description is assembled while
the program runs, every time it runs. A macro does the work once, before the
program starts, and leaves nothing behind.

One description can then produce several models. @sec-reaction-networks turns
the network above into a system of differential equations, a stochastic
differential equation, and a jump process, without restating the transmission
assumptions three times.

The cost is error messages about code you did not write. When a macro reports a
problem at a line that does not appear in your file, the line is in the
generated code, and `@macroexpand` is how you find out what it was.

### Differentiating code you wrote yourself

Several later chapters need derivatives. How far does the epidemic peak move if
$\beta$ moves a little? Fitting a model to data, finding the intervention with
the lowest cost, and the sampler used in @sec-bayesian-inference all work by
following the derivative of some quantity with respect to the parameters.

There are three ways to get one. Differentiate by hand and write the result
out, which is exact, error-prone, and has to be redone whenever the model
changes. Approximate it as $(f(\beta + h) - f(\beta))/h$ for some small $h$,
which is easy and loses accuracy. Or use *automatic differentiation*: have the
computer apply the chain rule to the operations your program performs,
which is accurate to the same precision as the original calculation and needs
no algebra from you.

The Julia version of the third option works through the type system rather than
through a separate library of operations. `ForwardDiff` defines a number type
called a *dual number* that carries two values, the quantity itself and its
derivative, with arithmetic defined so the second slot accumulates the chain
rule [@revels2016]. Because the kernel says nothing about what kind of number
`S` is, calling it with dual numbers runs the same source code and returns
derivatives alongside the rates:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-forwarddiff
using ForwardDiff

function new_infection_rate(β)
    du = zeros(eltype(β), 3)
    sir_ode!(du, u0, merge(p, (β = β,)), 0.0)
    return du[2]
end

ForwardDiff.derivative(new_infection_rate, p.β)
```

Nothing was written twice: `sir_ode!` is the function from the top of this
section, unchanged.

The value is checkable by hand, and worth checking the first time you use this.
Differentiating $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t = \beta c S I / N - \gamma I$ with
respect to $\beta$ leaves $c S I / N$, which at the baseline state is
$10 \times 990 \times 10 / 1000$:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-forwarddiff-check
analytic = p.c * u0[1] * u0[2] / p.N
(analytic, ForwardDiff.derivative(new_infection_rate, p.β) ≈ analytic)
```

That agreement is not the agreement of a good approximation. A finite
difference $(f(\beta + h) - f(\beta))/h$ has to trade truncation error against
rounding error in the choice of $h$; here the chain rule was applied to the
operations the kernel performs, so there is no $h$ to choose.

This is a different arrangement from the one used by PyTorch, JAX and
TensorFlow, which you may know from machine learning. Those libraries supply a
fixed catalogue of array operations with hand-written derivatives attached, and
can differentiate a program only to the extent that it is written in that
catalogue. A model written in plain NumPy cannot be differentiated by PyTorch
until it is rewritten in `torch` operations. The catalogue is large and well
optimised, so for the neural networks it was designed around this is seldom a
limitation. It becomes one when the thing you want to differentiate is a stiff
solver, an adaptive timestep controller, or the epidemic model you wrote last
week. Applying differentiation to the language instead of to a library is the
design Julia takes [@innes2019]. `Enzyme` pushes it further down, to the
intermediate representation the compiler produces on the way to machine code,
which lets it differentiate functions that overwrite their arguments and code
originally written in C or Fortran [@moses2020].

Two directions are available, and the choice is about shape rather than
accuracy. *Forward mode* carries derivatives along with the calculation and
costs one pass per input parameter: cheap for a model with three parameters,
expensive for one with three thousand. *Reverse mode* runs the calculation and
then walks it backwards, costing roughly one pass however many parameters there
are, at the price of storing intermediate results. Fitting a handful of
epidemiological parameters is forward-mode work; training the neural network
inside a universal differential equation, in the appendix of that name, is
reverse-mode work.

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not pin a model kernel to `Float64`

Automatic differentiation works by calling your function with a number type it
has not seen before, so anything that insists on `Float64` refuses those
numbers. The array written into is the usual culprit:

```julia
du = zeros(3)                  # Vector{Float64}: blocks AD
du = zeros(eltype(β), 3)       # matches whatever the caller passed
```

A signature can do the same damage:

```julia
function sir_ode!(du::Vector{Float64}, u::Vector{Float64}, p, t)  # blocks AD
```

The kernels written out in these chapters leave those types unwritten. This
follows from the dispatch section above, and it is the most common reason a
model that simulates correctly cannot then be fitted. The error names the type
it could not build, `MethodError: no method matching
Float64(::ForwardDiff.Dual{...})`, which is worth recognising on sight.

One exception is worth knowing about, because its signature does not show it.
`EpiModelingCourse.sir_ode!`, the shared copy of this kernel, converts the
parameters it is given into the `SIRParameters` type, whose fields are declared
`Float64`. It still differentiates with respect to the state, which it reads
straight out of `u`, but not with respect to a parameter — and a parameter is
what fitting, sensitivity analysis and optimisation all differentiate against.
Use the kernel as written above when you want that derivative.
:::

### Why the pieces fit together

The three features above are one argument, not three. Independently written
packages combine because of dispatch, because library code is written against
abstract types such as `Number` and `AbstractArray` rather than `Float64`, and
because a macro can generate code that other packages then consume. That is why
a reaction network written with one package can be differentiated by another
whose author never heard of it.

Composability does not mean any two Julia packages work together. It means the
work needed is usually adding methods rather than converting data. R achieves a
good deal of the same thing by other means: S3 and S4 generics dispatch on the
first argument, and the community's shared commitment to `data.frame` means
most analysis packages pipe into each other cleanly. R dispatches on one
argument and by convention; Julia dispatches on all of them and in the
compiler, so a new type meets an old solver more often without either side
being modified.

### Working alongside R, Python and C

Adopting Julia for a model does not require moving anything else. Julia calls
R, Python, C and Fortran from inside a Julia session, and R and Python call
Julia in return.

- `RCall.jl` runs R code and moves data across. `R"..."` sends a string to an R
  session, and `@rget` and `@rput` move variables between the two. Your
  cleaning pipeline, your `ggplot2` figures and the R package your group has
  relied on for years stay where they are.
- `PythonCall.jl` does the same for Python, and its companion `juliacall` lets
  a Python script call Julia.
- The `JuliaCall` R package is the reverse direction for R, so a colleague can
  call your Julia model without learning Julia.
- `ccall` reaches a function in a compiled C or Fortran library directly, with
  no intermediate layer. In most languages, making a C library available means
  writing glue in C and compiling it; here it is one expression naming the
  library, the function, and the argument types, and no C of your own. It is
  how a package such as `Sundials.jl` reaches an established numerical library:
  the package is a Julia wrapper around `ccall`s, not a compiled shim.

Every crossing converts data, so a loop calling R once per iteration will be
slow. You have two package environments to install and keep working, which is
where most of the trouble starts. An error raised on the far side arrives with
a stack trace from the other language.

Adoption can therefore be partial: one model kernel in Julia, called from the
pipeline you already have. None of these packages is used elsewhere in this
course, which keeps the course environment to one language.

### Reproducible randomness

Later chapters simulate stochastic epidemics. To make results reproducible we
seed a *local* random stream with `StableRNGs`, whose output is fixed across
Julia versions, unlike the global `Random.default_rng()`.

Two separate things are being bought here. Seeding a *local* stream means an
unrelated draw elsewhere in your session cannot shift the numbers this code
sees, which is what makes a result repeatable when you rerun a notebook out of
order. `StableRNG` then fixes the stream itself, so the same seed gives the same
draws on another machine and another Julia version. What neither guarantees is
that everything computed *from* those draws matches bit for bit everywhere:
floating-point arithmetic can reorder across platforms and library versions, so
an identical stream can still produce answers that differ in the last digits.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-rng
using StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
draws = rand(rng, 5)
```

### A figure from code

We now visualise @eq-p01-rate with `CairoMakie`. The last expression in the cell
(the `Figure`) is what Quarto renders.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-p01-rate
#| fig-cap: "Probability of at least one event in a window of width $\\delta t$ for a Poisson process, for a fast ($r=1$) and slow ($r=0.25$) rate. Both curves rise from 0 and saturate at 1."
using CairoMakie

fig = Figure(size = (640, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1];
    xlabel = "time step δt",
    ylabel = "event probability  1 − exp(−r δt)",
    title  = "Rate-to-proportion conversion")
lines!(ax, δts, p_fast; linewidth = 3, label = "r = 1.0")
lines!(ax, δts, p_slow; linewidth = 3, label = "r = 0.25")
axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
fig
```

## Validation

Two structural checks confirm the constructs behave as the mathematics
requires.

First, the derivatives in @eq-p01-sir must sum to zero, reproducing the
conservation law @eq-p01-conservation:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-check-conservation
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)
isapprox(sum(du), 0.0; atol = 1e-12)
```

Second, `rate_to_proportion` must reduce to its first-order Taylor expansion
$p \approx r\,\delta t$ as $\delta t \to 0$, and must return a valid probability
in $[0, 1]$ for every rate $r \ge 0$ and window $\delta t \ge 0$:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-check-rate
small = rate_to_proportion(0.25, 1e-6)
(isapprox(small, 0.25e-6; rtol = 1e-3), all(0 .<= p_fast .<= 1))
```

Both cells return `true`, so the in-place kernel conserves population and the
rate conversion is well behaved on the range it is used over.

## Interpretation and limitations

You now have the exact Julia vocabulary the course relies on: the REPL, in-place
kernels, broadcasting and comprehensions, loops that collect into arrays, named
tuples read by field and updated with `merge`, dispatch, and seeded randomness.
This unit is deliberately narrow: it is not a full Julia tutorial. It does not
cover package management beyond activating and
instantiating the course environment, performance profiling,
user-defined `struct`s, or the type system's parametric machinery. Macros are
covered only far enough to read one and expand it; writing your own is needed
nowhere in this course. Automatic differentiation is described here but
exercised later, in @sec-sensitivity-and-identifiability and the universal
differential equations appendix. For those, consult the official
[Julia documentation](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/) and the
[performance tips](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/).
The [CairoMakie documentation](https://docs.makie.org/stable/) covers the
plotting API in depth.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#p01-ex1}

Write an in-place kernel `sir_incidence!(du, u, p, t)` that extends
@eq-p01-sir with a fourth state $C$ tracking *cumulative* infections, so that
$\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}t = \lambda S$. Evaluate the derivative at the baseline
initial condition extended with $C(0) = 0$, so that $C$ counts infections
occurring after $t = 0$:

```julia
u0_incidence = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]
```

Confirm that `du[4]` equals `-du[1]`: new infections leave $S$ at exactly the
rate they are added to the cumulative count.

### Exercise 2 {#p01-ex2}

Using `StableRNG(2024)`, draw 10 000 samples with `rand(rng, 10_000)`, and count
how many fall below `rate_to_proportion(0.25, 1.0)`. Compare the observed
fraction with the target probability, then explain what a *local* seeded
`StableRNG` guarantees about this result on another machine, and what it does
not.
